body:
This looks pretty good.

My understanding is that `ValuePtr` is an abstraction to allow deep copies of a dynamic object so that the owning object doesn't have to handle all the bug prone stuff and memory management itself.

The difference from `std::indirect` is that `ValuePtr` can be NULL, which allows not using that memory on objects that don't need this extra data.

I believe the same can be achieved with the `std::indirect` by using it in combination with `std::optional`, but `ValuePtr` is more suited for purposes here.

Just querying that point above before approve.

(I might well have used this pattern before probably in Godot but with raw pointers (maybe for some interpolation data?), so might check over whether there's anything prior that can be replaced with `ValuePtr`).

> This looks pretty good.
> 
> My understanding is that `ValuePtr` is an abstraction to allow deep copies of a dynamic object so that the owning object doesn't have to handle all the bug prone stuff and memory management itself.
> 
> The difference from `std::indirect` is that `ValuePtr` can be NULL, which allows not using that memory on objects that don't need this extra data.

Yea, that's a difference.
(look at me, a `nullptr` hater, making a `nullptr` type 😅)

> I believe the same can be achieved with the `std::indirect` by using it in combination with `std::optional`, but `ValuePtr` is more suited for purposes here.

Behaviourally, yes. But it would defeat the purpose of the PR. 

`std::indirect<std::optional<T>>` will always allocate, and it will allocate for `std::optional<T>` which is `sizeof(T) + sizeof(bool)`. I believe Rust optimizes for this exact case with nullpointer surrogate values, but I'm pretty sure the C++ compiler wouldn't be allowed to.
